title: Ποιμὴν καὶ λύκος ⟨σὺν κυσὶ τρεφόμενος⟩
titleEn: The Shepherd and the Wolf Reared with the Dogs
part: The Shepherd and the Wolf Reared with the Dogs (Chambry 314)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 314. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ποιμὴν νεογνὸν λύκου σκύμνον εὑρὼν καὶ ἀνελόμενος σὺν τοῖς κυσὶν ἔτρεφεν.
sentences.tr: Poimēn neognon lykou skymnon heurōn kai anelomenos syn tois kysin etrephen.
sentences.l: A shepherd, having found a newborn cub of a wolf and having taken him up, reared him along with the dogs.
sentences.n: ἀναιρέομαι in the middle is to take a foundling up for oneself, the word used of rescuing an exposed child. σκύμνος is the cub of any beast, and λύκου is the possessive genitive that names which. Chambry supplies the descriptive half of the title, ⟨σὺν κυσὶ τρεφόμενος⟩, in his angle brackets for words he adds.

sentences.t: Ἐπεὶ δὲ ηὐξήθη, εἴ ποτε λύκος πρόβατον ἥρπασε, μετὰ τῶν κυνῶν καὶ αὐτὸς ἐδίωκε.
sentences.tr: Epei de ēuxēthē, ei pote lykos probaton hērpase, meta tōn kynōn kai autos ediōke.
sentences.l: And when he had grown, if ever a wolf snatched a sheep, he too would give chase along with the dogs.
sentences.n: εἴ ποτε with the aorist indicative and an imperfect in the main clause states what used to happen whenever it happened. The regular classical shape of this past general condition puts the optative in the εἰ-clause, as the fourth sentence does with ἀρπάσειε; the indicative here is the looser later usage. καὶ αὐτός is 'he too', the wolf falling in with the dogs.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ κυνῶν ἔσθ’ ὅτε μὴ δυναμένων καταλαβεῖν τὸν λύκον καὶ διὰ ταῦτα ὑποστρεφόντων, ἐκεῖνος ἠκολούθει, μέχρις ἂν τοῦτον καταλαβών, οἷα δὴ λύκος, συμμετάσχῃ τῆς θήρας· εἶτα ὑπέστρεφεν.
sentences.tr: Tōn de kynōn esth’ hote mē dynamenōn katalabein ton lykon kai dia tauta hypostrephontōn, ekeinos ēkolouthei, mechris an touton katalabōn, hoia dē lykos, symmetaschēi tēs thēras· eita hypestrephen.
sentences.l: But the dogs being at times unable to overtake the wolf and for that reason turning back, that one kept following, until, having overtaken it — being of course a wolf himself — he might share in the quarry; then he would turn back.
sentences.i: Sometimes the dogs could not catch the wolf and would turn back on that account, but he kept on after it, until he had run it down and, being a wolf after all, had his share of the kill; then he would come back.
sentences.n: ἔσθ’ ὅτε, literally 'there are times when', is a fixed phrase for 'sometimes'. μέχρις ἄν with the subjunctive sets the limit of a repeated action. οἷα δή with a noun gives a reason from what a thing is — 'seeing that he was a wolf'. συμμετέχω takes the genitive of what is shared.

sentences.t: Εἰ δὲ μὴ λύκος ἔξωθεν ἀρπάσειε πρόβατον, αὐτὸς λάθρᾳ θύων ἅμα τοῖς κυσὶν ἐθοινεῖτο, ἕως ὁ ποιμὴν στοχασάμενος καὶ συνεὶς τὸ δρώμενον, εἰς δένδρον αὐτὸν ἀναρτήσας ἀπέκτεινεν.
sentences.tr: Ei de mē lykos exōthen arpaseie probaton, autos lathrāi thyōn hama tois kysin ethoineito, heōs ho poimēn stochasamenos kai syneis to drōmenon, eis dendron auton anartēsas apekteinen.
sentences.l: But if no wolf from outside snatched a sheep, he himself, slaughtering one secretly, would feast on it together with the dogs, until the shepherd, guessing and understanding what was being done, having hung him on a tree, killed him.
sentences.i: But if no wolf from outside took a sheep, he would kill one himself on the sly and make a feast of it along with the dogs — until the shepherd worked out what was going on, strung him up on a tree, and killed him.
sentences.n: εἰ with the optative and an imperfect in the main clause is the past general condition in its regular form, and negative here. Chambry prints ἀρπάσειε with a smooth breathing, where ἥρπασε two sentences above has the rough one that ἁρπάζω regularly takes; both stand as printed. θύω is properly to sacrifice, and stands here for simply killing a beast for the eating. στοχάζομαι is to aim at a mark, hence to guess. τὸ δρώμενον, the present passive participle under the article, is 'the thing being done'.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι φύσις πονηρὰ χρηστὸν ἦθος οὐ τρέφει.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti physis ponēra chrēston ēthos ou trephei.
sentences.l: The fable shows that a wicked nature does not rear a good character.
sentences.n: τρέφει takes up the ἔτρεφεν of the story: the shepherd did the rearing, but the moral says nature does the real rearing. ἦθος is settled character, as against φύσις, the nature one is born with.
